narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 71.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your first-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is well below the average of sixth decile among students who were accepted, signaling that your early performance was significantly weaker than most successful applicants. Your third-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure, though with less force; you ranked in the third decile compared with an average around the sixth among accepted students. Finally, your undergraduate GPA of 2.80 contributed a smaller but still negative push; it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of admitted students.

Taken together, these academic signals outweighed other information such as your LSAT score of 35, your high family income, and your plan to attend full-time. The model therefore concluded that the risk of bar exam failure was too high to offer admission.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake challenging courses, improve your study habits, and aim to raise both your class rank and GPA before reapplying. Consider targeted bar-prep resources early so that when you retake the exam your first-attempt success rate improves. With clearer evidence of academic growth, your next application will look very different to the model. (248 words)
